    How this workspace works
    These are real C programs compiled to WebAssembly and run on your device. This is a command runner with a flat shared filesystem. It supports arguments, preloaded standard input, multiple C sources, and local headers. It does not provide a Unix shell, pipes, networking, or native Linux executables. Use Codespaces for native tools and threads.
    The TinyDB prompt runs the included C program for each statement against the same file. INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, and COUNT are supported for the people table; each successful mutation commits immediately. It is a teaching database with 128 rows, scans, and a bounded binary format. It has no transactions, indexes, concurrent writers, or crash-durability guarantee. Its source also runs as a stdin REPL in Codespaces.
    Files save in this browser using IndexedDB. Download important files; clearing site data removes them. Files are separate from lesson drafts and completion. Limits: 32 files, 2 MB per file, 8 MB total, 256 KB per C source, 100 KB output, and 5 seconds per run (up to 2 minutes to prepare the compiler). Stopping or trapping retains the files from before the command. A normal nonzero exit still saves file changes.

    05

    Add a write-ahead log and simulate interrupted writes.
    Small on purpose
    The command workspace includes a runnable C TinyDB with INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, and persistent binary files. The course also teaches indexes, transactions, and recovery as separate models to assemble into your own project. Run TinyDB in the CLI →
    

    ← Chapter 11: Correctness and Big O
    How does the work grow?
    Search a sorted list of integers for its last value. Count one comparison each time we inspect an element.
    Linear search checks every element. Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining range.
    Try a larger list
    For this example, doubling the list doubles linear search’s comparisons, while binary search needs one extra comparison. This illustrates linear O(n) and logarithmic O(log n) growth. Both iterative searches use O(1) extra space.
    Other growth rates and formal notation
    Big O describes an asymptotic upper bound, not an exact runtime. We also use Θ for a tight asymptotic bound and Ω for a lower bound. Always specify the input size, assumptions, and case being analyzed.
    GrowthExample
    O(1)Read one array element by index
    O(log n)Binary search: worst-case time on sorted data
    O(n)Scan an entire array
    O(n log n)Merge sort: worst-case time
    O(n²)Insertion sort: worst-case time
    These growth classes omit constant factors. Algorithm, input order, implementation, and hardware affect actual timings. Auxiliary space is analyzed separately.

    ← Complete course
    Choose where to run C
    Every chapter is readable in the browser, including on a tablet. The execution label describes the chapter’s project environment, not a requirement for reading.
    Browser labs
    The fifteen available exercises compile and run in this page using WebAssembly. Your edits and checked exercises stay in this browser. Lesson-run files are temporary. The command workspace keeps shared files between runs and supports import and export. All 226 topic readings include complete examples and questions. Example runs and self-marked completion are separate from graded practice output checks.
    Codespaces labs
    Use GitHub Codespaces for multi-file builds, debugging and sanitizers, compiler standards experiments, threads, and the native TinyDB project. It runs Linux and the editor in a browser; a desktop computer is not required.
    1. Open a chapter’s Codespaces link and sign in to GitHub.
    2. Wait for the dev container to finish installing the toolchains and checking the native foundations.
    3. Paste the chapter’s command into the terminal. It shows the workspace plan and the available starting points.
    4. Edit the files in that workspace and run the relevant build or test command.
    The repository contains complete native examples alongside five earlier foundations and two editable Part 2 projects. Later lessons include bounded executable models of indexes, recovery, snapshots, and richer queries. Assembling these components into a complete database remains learner project work.
    Writing portable C
    Part 7 covers portable files, text, parsing, encodings, paths, and explicit host interfaces. Finish with the TinyDB portability audit. Run make check-portability in Codespaces or locally; Windows users can run python tools/check_portability.py --compiler cl in an MSVC developer terminal. The Actions matrix tests Linux GCC/Clang, macOS Clang, and Windows MSVC and exchanges their database files. These checks qualify the audited target; OS-specific course components have their own requirements.
    Optional debugging labs
    GDB is preinstalled in the Codespaces image. At the end of Part 2, investigate a small C bug using breakpoints, stepping, variables, the call stack, and a watchpoint. At the end of Part 6, repair a broken TinyDB and verify its saved rows. Run make debug-gdb LAB=basics or make debug-gdb LAB=tinydb in the native terminal. Local Linux/WSL works too. These sessions are optional; the browser command workspace does not run GDB.
    Keep your work
    Use your own fork or branch and commit and push changes you want to keep. A Codespace’s files persist across stops, but unpushed work can be lost when the Codespace is deleted. Browser drafts are not transferred automatically: use Export to download main.c, then upload or paste it into your Codespace.
    If you already have a Codespace, reuse it from your Codespaces list. Codespaces uses your GitHub account’s compute and storage allowance; check the current terms. Stop it when finished; deleting it releases its stored workspace usage.
    Local development
    Clone the repository and reopen it in an editor supporting dev containers, or install GCC/Clang, Make, Python 3, and Node 24 locally. The same commands work in either environment.
    make check-native
make check-native-clang
make standards-matrix
make sanitize
make serve

    UNDER THE HOOD
    A real browser C lab.
    Clang and LLD are compiled to WebAssembly. Your source compiles and runs locally in a Web Worker. No compilation server is involved.
    This prototype uses the experimental wasm-clang toolchain. It supports C17 and a subset of WASI. Native processes, sockets, and some system APIs are unavailable. Programs have a 5-second execution limit; standard input is provided before running.
    Source, input, and completed lessons are saved in this browser. Lesson-run files are temporary; the command workspace saves files in this browser. Output checks are practice aids, not a security-grade assessment.
